tldr: By interpreting the joint mesh of a human and an object generated by a Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) as a geometric scaffold, this work achieves high-accuracy monocular 3D interaction reconstruction without relying on contact annotations or predefined CAD templates.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of MILO. From a monocular RGB image, an LRM (Hunyuan3D-2.0) generates a joint human-object mesh. Through multi-view renderings, 3D keypoint estimation/human body model fitting and point cloud segmentation (with optional template alignment) are performed in parallel.
overview:
Understanding how humans interact with objects (HOI) in 3D from a single image is essential for robot imitation learning and AR/VR. However, 3D reconstruction from a monocular camera is an extremely challenging problem due to severe depth ambiguities, occlusions, and large object shape variability. Many existing methods rely on 2D reprojection constraints, manually annotated contact labels, or template retrieval from known CAD shape libraries, which severely limits their real-world generalization.

To address this, the authors made a key observation: "Can a Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) yield a 3D mesh that inherently preserves the relative spatial arrangement and proximity cues between humans and objects in one shot?" By treating the joint mesh produced by the LRM as a "geometric scaffold," they reframed the problem from fitting models to 2D images into interpreting and decomposing the LRM mesh into human and object parts. In the proposed framework, MILO, a parametric human body model (SMPL-H) is fitted to the LRM mesh, and the object point cloud is extracted via segmentation (with optional template alignment when CAD models are available).

Experiments on multiple benchmarks (InterCap, HODome, IMHD) and in-the-wild images (PICO-db) demonstrate that MILO achieves geometric consistency and physical plausibility that significantly outperform conventional baselines, even without ground-truth contact labels or prior templates.
contributions: Formulated a new paradigm that treats the joint mesh generated by a Large Reconstruction Model (LRM) as a geometric scaffold, reframing monocular 3D interaction reconstruction into an LRM mesh interpretation task.
Established a robust framework that stably fits the SMPL-H human body model to the LRM mesh via 3D keypoint triangulation from multi-view renderings and an occlusion-resilient two-stage optimization.

Achieved state-of-the-art reconstruction accuracy that significantly outperforms existing optimization- and regression-based baselines without relying on ground-truth contact information or CAD templates.

sections.heading: Moving Away from 2D Reprojection: A New Idea to "Interpret" LRM 3D Meshes
sections.summary: Reconstructing 3D human-object interactions from a single image is notoriously difficult due to occlusions and diverse object shapes. This paper proposes MILO, a framework that leverages the joint human-object mesh generated by an LRM as a geometric scaffold, recovering detailed 3D interactions with high accuracy without relying on contact labels.
sections.details:
Daily human activities constantly involve contact and manipulation with diverse objects such as tools and furniture. While 3D HOI understanding is indispensable for robot teleoperation and Embodied AI, estimating it from monocular images is always plagued by depth ambiguity and occlusions.

Powerful parametric models like SMPL exist for the human body, but there is no unified representation for generic objects. Consequently, existing methods have been forced to either retrieve similar shapes from large CAD databases or rely on privileged inputs such as ground-truth contact annotations or depth maps.

The core insight of this work is that LRMs pretrained on massive data already encode rich relative spatial arrangements and proximity cues between humans and objects within their 3D meshes. By shifting away from the quagmire of optimizing against 2D reprojection errors and instead interpreting a single joint mesh produced by an LRM, the uncertainty of the problem is dramatically reduced.

captions.F1: Conceptual overview of MILO. From an input photo, an LRM predicts a joint mesh uniting human and object. By decomposing and interpreting this mesh into human and object components, coherent 3D interaction geometry is reconstructed.

sections.heading: Context of Human/Object Reconstruction and Contact Estimation, and MILO's Place
sections.summary: The paper organizes prior work across monocular human reconstruction, 3D object reconstruction, and contact estimation. Unlike earlier studies that only applied LRMs to objects, MILO fundamentally differs by applying the LRM to the entire joint scene containing both human and object to capture their relative relationship.
sections.details:
Research in monocular 3D reconstruction can be largely divided into three streams:

- Monocular 3D human reconstruction: Optimization approaches fitting parametric models like SMPL and SMPL-X, as well as deep regression models like HMR2.0, have progressed significantly. However, these focus only on isolated humans and disregard contact with surrounding objects.

- Monocular 3D object reconstruction and LRMs: Following NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting, LRMs trained on large datasets (such as Hunyuan3D-2.0) have emerged, enabling accurate and fast reconstruction of diverse object geometries.

- 3D HOI reconstruction and contact estimation: Previous works (CONTHO, CHORE, PICO, etc.) relied on predicting contact maps or learning dense correspondences. While some efforts like EasyHOI used LRMs for object reconstruction, they reconstructed the isolated object separately before fitting it to the image, making contact labels indispensable to determine relative placement.

In contrast, MILO prompts the LRM to generate both the human and the object simultaneously as a single joint mesh. This provides a natural guarantee of their mutual geometric relationship without requiring explicit contact annotations or CAD templates.

sections.heading: The Algorithm for Untangling Human and Object from the Scaffold Mesh
sections.summary: From the joint mesh generated by the LRM, multi-view virtual renderings are used to perform 3D keypoint estimation and segmentation. Based on these cues, two-stage optimization of the human body (root and pose) and object separation (along with optional template alignment) are executed.
sections.details:
MILO's processing pipeline consists of the following steps:

3.1 Human Body Model Definition
The SMPL-H model, which includes hands, is adopted. From global orientation $\Phi$, body pose $\Theta$, hand pose $\Theta_h$, shape $\beta$, and translation $\Gamma$, a 6,890-vertex mesh and 52 joint locations are computed.

3.2 Joint Mesh Generation with LRM
An RGBA image with the background removed is fed into Hunyuan3D-2.0 to generate a unified mesh containing both human and object. This is treated as the "geometric scaffold" of the interaction.

3.3 3D Keypoint Estimation
60 virtual viewpoints are arranged around the joint mesh to produce rendered images. ViTPose (25 full-body points) and HaMeR (21 points per hand) are applied to each view. Robust multi-view triangulation and non-linear optimization yield a confidence-weighted set of 3D keypoints $X \in \mathbb{R}^{67 \times 3}$.

3.4 Human Body Optimization (Two-Stage Fitting)
The SMPL-H model initialized with HMR2.0 and HaMeR is aligned to the LRM mesh.
- Root fitting: Body pose, hand pose, and shape are fixed, and only global rotation $\Phi$, translation $\Gamma$, and an unknown scale factor are optimized for 30 iterations using a robust loss function (Geman-McClure).
- Pose fitting: All parameters are unfreezed. In addition to pose and shape priors (VPoser, MANO, L2), a "soft-anchor loss to HMR initialization" to address occlusion hallucinations and a "one-way Chamfer loss on visible vertices" are introduced for 60 iterations of optimization.

3.5 Point Cloud Segmentation
Rendered images are prompted with "person.<obj_name>" to obtain segmentation masks, which are back-projected and aggregated onto mesh vertices using viewpoint quality scores and boundary distance weighting. Non-human clusters are extracted and cleaned via geometric filtering to yield the object point cloud.

3.6 Template Alignment (Optional)
When a CAD model is available, a geometric correspondence model (Zhang et al.) extracts semantic correspondences between LRM renderings and template renderings. Filtered by bidirectional cycle consistency, sparse 3D correspondences compute a similarity transformation (Sim(3)), followed by ICP for precise alignment.

captions.F3: Template alignment pipeline. In the top row, a geometric correspondence model detects semantic correspondences between template renderings and LRM renderings. In the bottom row, iterative Sim(3) fitting aligns the template accurately to the LRM object point cloud.

sections.heading: Achieving SOTA Without Ground-Truth Contact: Validating the Geometric Scaffold
sections.summary: Quantitative and qualitative evaluations were conducted across InterCap, HODome, and IMHD datasets. Even without contact information, MILO outperforms existing methods in geometric accuracy, and ablations confirm the necessity of using a joint mesh.
sections.details:
Experiments were evaluated under rigorous protocols.

4.1 Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods
On the InterCap benchmark, Procrustes-aligned Chamfer Distance (PA-CD) was evaluated for human, object, and the joint pair (h+o). Even in the template-free setting (PA-CD h+o: 6.90 cm), MILO outperformed existing methods such as CONTHO (11.51 cm) and PICO (7.61 cm), which use object templates or ground-truth contact information. With template alignment, accuracy improved to 6.53 cm. MILO also surpassed PICO on HODome and IMHD datasets.

4.2 Downstream Impact on Contact Estimation
Although MILO is not trained on explicit contact labels, predicting contact based on the distance between reconstructed human and object surfaces (< 5 mm) yielded a higher F1 score (0.687 vs. 0.654) and lower geometric error (1.06 cm vs. 1.25 cm) than DECO (trained on RICH), a model specialized for contact prediction.

4.3 Impact of Mesh Geometry and LRM Choice
Replacing the LRM backbone with SAM3D achieved similarly high accuracy, demonstrating independence from a specific model. In an oracle experiment using ground-truth meshes as input, errors were further halved, showing that future advances in LRMs will directly boost MILO's performance.

4.4 Joint Reconstruction vs. Independent Reconstruction (Key Ablation)
Compared to an "independent baseline (SAM3D independent)" that reconstructs human and object separately and merges them via depth maps, MILO using a joint mesh was overwhelmingly superior (PA-CD h+o: 6.90 cm vs. 13.91 cm). This proves that the "scaffold" jointly reconstructed by the LRM is fundamentally critical for determining relative positioning and scale.

4.5 Qualitative Evaluation and In-The-Wild Images
On in-the-wild PICO-db images, MILO reliably reconstructs physically plausible interaction geometry without extreme human-object interpenetration or floating artifacts.

captions.F4: Qualitative comparison on the InterCap dataset. From left to right: input image, CONTHO, HOI-TG, PICO, MILO (w/ and w/o template), and ground-truth mesh. MILO suppresses unnatural object tilts and penetrations seen in other methods, reconstructing 3D arrangements closest to ground truth.
captions.F5: Comparison with PICO on HODome and IMHD datasets. In scenes involving holding or sitting on chairs, suitcases, and pans, MILO exhibits high physical plausibility even without templates (orange mesh).
captions.F6: Qualitative results on in-the-wild images (PICO-db). Plausible 3D interactions are successfully reconstructed across diverse categories and complex poses, including bicycles, backpacks, and baseball gloves.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook: LRM-Driven Label-Free HOI Understanding
sections.summary: By treating an LRM as a geometric scaffold, MILO achieves highly generalizable 3D human-object interaction reconstruction without contact labels. Future directions include mitigating dependency on LRM geometric quality and expanding to video and multi-person interactions.
sections.details:
This work proposed a paradigm that leverages the global 3D geometry generated by LRMs as a prior for reconstructing human-object interactions from monocular images. The breakthrough lies in transforming the ill-posed problem of "fitting via 2D reprojection" into "interpreting a global mesh."

Limitations and future challenges include:
- Reliance on LRM quality: For very small objects or under heavy occlusion, LRMs may fail to reconstruct fine details, leading to segmentation failures.
- Ambiguity with symmetric objects: During template alignment, highly symmetric objects (such as boxes or bottles) can experience 180-degree flipped orientations.
- Extension to temporal and multi-person settings: Currently specialized for single-image, single-pair scenarios, extending to video input and simultaneous tracking of multiple humans and objects is the next step.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Details, Runtime Analysis, and Failure Cases
sections.summary: The appendix details hyperparameters for virtual viewpoint generation and robust triangulation, runtimes for each stage, and ablation studies on point cloud segmentation.
sections.details:
The appendix provides practical implementation details and additional analyses:

- Implementation hyperparameters: Virtual viewpoint rendering is performed across 60 views with 30-degree azimuth steps and elevations of 0, ±30, and ±60 degrees. Keypoint triangulation employs a confidence threshold >= 0.6 and a reprojection error threshold of 5.0 pixels. Mesh segmentation incorporates penalty weights via morphological dilation near contact boundaries.

- Runtime analysis: On an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada GPU, the core pipeline (without templates) takes 344.40 seconds per image. LRM mesh generation (130.40 s) and multi-view rendering (148 s) account for most of the runtime. Keypoint estimation, fitting, and segmentation take 66 seconds in total; notably, human body optimization takes only 32.3 seconds, which is significantly faster than PICO's optimization (475.84 s). When optional template alignment is performed, correspondence search requires an additional 375.75 seconds.

- Failure case analysis: Key error sources include cases where the LRM misidentifies boundaries and incorporates background regions, scale inaccuracies on thin or elongated objects (e.g., bats or umbrellas), and rotational flips on symmetric geometries.

takeaways: Using an LRM as a "geometric scaffold" to preserve global relative placement and scale is an extremely powerful approach for monocular multi-object and human arrangements.

Decomposing a joint mesh co-generated by an LRM dramatically suppresses contact penetrations and scale mismatches compared to reconstructing humans and objects independently and merging them via depth maps.

Rendering multi-view virtual views from a 3D mesh, applying 2D foundation models, and triangulating provides a versatile pipeline for extracting accurate parametric models from imperfect generative meshes.
limitations: Because it relies on LRM generation fidelity, missing geometry or hallucinations frequently occur for very small objects or under severe occlusions.
When aligning templates to perfectly symmetric or rotationally symmetric objects, a failure mode exists where the orientation converges to a 180-degree flip.
Due to multi-view rendering and semantic correspondence searching, the pipeline currently requires several minutes per frame, preventing immediate application to real-time robot control.
